title: Die-level DRAM harvesting from retired server DIMMs
idea: Po: chips are fruit you can pick twice. Retired hyperscaler DIMMs are depackaged at die level (laser ablation of mold compound plus selective wet etch of wires/RDL), dies are re-probed and re-binned as known-good-die, then restacked into new 4-8-high fan-out packages with fresh SPD and ECC profiles.
why: Turns millions of retired DDR4/early-DDR5 modules a year into supply with near-zero wafer capex; harvest cost per bit ~20-30% of new silicon if post-decap die yield >70%; attacks capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability (harvest plants can be domestic).

title: Phone LPDDR packages reballed onto CXL bridge cards
idea: Po: every phone is a memory mine. Recyclers desolder LPDDR4X/5 packages from end-of-life phones (hot-gas rework plus automated reballing), test them on a fixture, and mount 16-32 of them on a CXL Type-3 card whose controller bridges the LPDDR protocol and masks per-package defects with a remap table.
why: >1B phones a year reach end of life holding 4-12 GB each; recovering even 10% yields billions of GB of capacity-tier memory for cold pages with zero wafer starts; attacks cost per bit and scarce capacity.

title: Bottle-deposit refunds on every gigabyte of DRAM
idea: Po: memory has a bottle deposit. A refundable deposit (e.g., $0.50/GB) is charged on DRAM-bearing devices and modules and refunded when they are returned to a certified harvester; unclaimed deposits fund harvest-plant capex.
why: Bottle-bill regions see 70-90% return rates versus ~20% e-waste collection; guarantees predictable feedstock so die/package harvesting can be financed; attacks scarce-resource intensity and supply.

title: Cross-tenant memory exchange points in colocation campuses
idea: Po: memory is a utility traded between strangers. Like an Internet exchange point, a neutral CXL 3.x switch fabric in each colo lets tenants post idle DRAM and others lease it by the GB-hour, with per-lease memory-encryption keys and bandwidth QoS enforced in the switch.
why: Fleet studies show ~25-50% of server DRAM stranded; turning 10% of it into tradeable supply equals a new fab's annual output; attacks effective cost per bit and capital.

title: Short-retention DRAM bins sold for ephemeral AI data
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen but pass at 16 or 32 ms are no longer scrapped; they are marked R16/R32 in SPD, priced lower, and paired with controllers that refresh 2-4x faster or host only data that lives <10 ms (activations, KV-cache scratch, network buffers).
why: Retention-tail failures are a major yield-loss bin; recovering them could add several percent sellable bits per wafer at zero capex; attacks cost per bit and supply.

title: Ship imperfect dies with a standardized bad-row map
idea: Po: every chip is broken. A JEDEC-style 'fault map in SPD' lets fabs ship dies with up to ~0.5% bad rows beyond on-die repair; BIOS/OS reads the map at boot and retires those physical pages, so dies now downgraded or scrapped become full-price product.
why: Raises good-die yield at leading nodes by an estimated 3-10%, i.e., free wafer capacity; attacks cost per bit and capital intensity.

title: Small-die variants that harvest partial reticle fields at wafer edge
idea: Po: the wafer edge is the most valuable land. The reticle carries the main 24-32 Gb die plus a 4-8 Gb small die built from the same array mats; partial fields at the wafer edge, normally lost, are diced into small dies for IoT, auto and embedded markets.
why: Edge loss is ~5-10% of wafer area for large dies; recovering half adds ~3-5% bits per wafer with no new tools; attacks cost per bit.

title: Move DRAM burn-in from the factory into the server
idea: Po: never test a chip in the factory. Factory test shrinks to wafer sort plus a fast package screen, and the long retention/burn-in screens run in the customer's server at first boot via on-die MBIST and post-package repair, with anonymized telemetry streamed back to the fab.
why: DRAM test and burn-in take hours per part and test floors are a large back-end capex; halving them frees test capacity and cuts cycle time by days; attacks capital intensity and time-to-supply.

title: Hyperscaler take-or-pay SPVs that own DRAM fab lines
idea: Po: the customer owns the fab. Like LNG trains financed by 20-year take-or-pay contracts, 3-5 hyperscalers fund a special-purpose vehicle that owns a DRAM line run by an incumbent or new entrant, receiving output at cost-plus in proportion to equity.
why: Contracted offtake lets fab debt be priced like infrastructure (~5-6%) instead of chip equity (~12-15%); with depreciation ~55% of wafer cost, a lower WACC cuts cost per bit ~15-25%; attacks capital intensity.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve that buys gluts and sells spikes
idea: Po: DRAM is oil. A government reserve buys known-good DRAM dies and modules during price troughs, stores them in nitrogen dry cabinets, and auctions them when contract prices rise more than ~50% year-over-year.
why: Smooths the boom-bust cycle that makes fabs underinvest: trough buying keeps fabs near full utilization and spike releases cap 4x price surges; attacks supply stability and capital risk.

title: Government-reinsured price-floor insurance for DRAM fab capex
idea: Po: memory prices cannot fall. Fabs buy a policy that pays out when a DRAM price index drops below a cash-cost floor, reinsured by a federal backstop like crop insurance, on condition that the fab keeps its committed capex schedule during the downturn.
why: Trough capex cuts are why shortages arrive 2-3 years later; insured fabs keep building, and lower revenue volatility reduces cost of capital; attacks capital intensity and supply timing.

title: Exchange-traded DRAM bit futures for long-dated hedging
idea: Po: bits are traded like wheat. A standardized cash-settled contract (e.g., 1 Tb of DDR5-equivalent per quarter against a published contract-price index) lets fabs sell output 3-5 years forward and buyers hedge, so a greenfield fab can be project-financed against hedged revenue.
why: Hedged revenue opens project finance to new entrants and cuts the risk premium over the 3-5-year build gap; attacks capital intensity.

title: Negabyte rebates that pay software to shrink memory footprint
idea: Po: memory is negative. Like utility negawatt programs, cloud providers and governments pay software vendors a rebate per GB-hour of verified footprint reduction (fleet telemetry against a baseline), funded by avoided DRAM purchases.
why: Software bloat is the cheapest supply source: 10-30% footprint cuts in ubiquitous runtimes (JVMs, browsers, databases) free capacity worth several fabs' output; attacks cost per usable bit.

title: Open-source DRAM process kit built from expired patents
idea: Po: the fab is open source. A consortium assembles a full 30-40 nm-class stacked-capacitor DRAM process flow and array/periphery design from patents that have expired, publishes it under an open license, and qualifies it at a U.S. specialty foundry for legacy DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4.
why: Removes the IP and know-how barrier that keeps DRAM a three-firm market; legacy grades still ship billions of units to auto/industrial; attacks U.S. manufacturability and supplier diversity.

title: Shortage-triggered compulsory licensing of DRAM patents
idea: Po: patents sleep during a shortage. When an official DRAM price index exceeds a threshold (e.g., 2x its 3-year average), any qualified domestic producer may practice listed DRAM patents at a tribunal-set royalty, using government-use and march-in style powers.
why: Removes the litigation risk that deters entrants exactly when entry is most needed; attacks supplier diversity and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Airbus-style allied DRAM company with stage-hosting by member nations
idea: Po: the factory belongs to many nations. Allied governments (e.g., U.S., Japan, EU, India) co-own one DRAM company in which each hosts a stage (front-end fab, test, packaging, stacking) and receives allocation proportional to equity, Airbus-style.
why: Splits the $15B+ fab ticket across sponsors and creates a fourth supplier outside today's three; attacks capital intensity and chokepoint concentration.

title: Shipyard-built fab modules assembled on site in 18 months
idea: Po: a fab is built in a year. Cleanroom bays, sub-fab utility skids and chemical distribution are built as standardized transportable modules in shipyards and factories (as LNG trains and offshore platforms are), then stacked on site under one frozen copy-exactly design.
why: Cuts fab construction from 3-5 years to ~18-24 months and construction cost ~20-30% through repetition; attacks the time and capital bottleneck.

title: Warehouse fab with sealed tool-to-tool nitrogen tunnels instead of cleanroom
idea: Po: the cleanroom is the size of a shoebox. Wafers never meet room air: a sealed N2 overhead tunnel links every tool load-port, so the building is an ordinary industrial warehouse instead of an ISO-class ballroom with massive filtration and HVAC.
why: Cleanroom shell and HVAC are a large share of fab construction cost and energy; removing the ballroom could cut building capex ~30% and HVAC energy ~50%; attacks capital and energy.

title: Co-site fabs on domestic helium fields with closed-loop recapture
idea: Po: the fab sits on a helium well. New DRAM fabs are sited at U.S. helium-bearing gas fields (Kansas/Texas Hugoton, Wyoming) with a dedicated cryogenic extraction plant, and every helium-using tool (backside cooling, leak check, purge) exhausts into a membrane-plus-PSA recapture loop.
why: Removes exposure to the Qatar outage (~30% of supply) and recaptures ~80-90% of fab helium; attacks scarce-resource intensity.

title: Synthetic fused-silica crucibles replacing Spruce Pine quartz
idea: Po: crucibles are made, not mined. Czochralski crucibles are slip-cast from synthetic silica made by flame hydrolysis of domestic SiCl4 (a polysilicon byproduct), with a barium-doped inner layer that mimics natural high-purity quartz devitrification behavior.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine chokepoint for the wafers DRAM is built on and recycles a polysilicon waste stream; attacks scarce-resource intensity.

title: Molybdenum wordlines and contacts mined in Colorado replace Chinese tungsten
idea: Po: tungsten is illegal. Buried wordlines, bitline contacts and periphery plugs switch from W to ALD/CVD molybdenum (lower resistivity at narrow widths, barrier-free on some layers), sourced from U.S. mines such as Climax and Henderson.
why: China supplies ~80% of tungsten while the U.S. is a top molybdenum producer; also trims wordline RC; attacks scarce-resource intensity and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Double-blind inventory clearinghouse to kill DRAM bullwhip hoarding
idea: Po: every warehouse is made of glass. A neutral party collects encrypted inventory and order data from DRAM makers, distributors and top buyers and, via secure multiparty computation, publishes only weekly aggregate true-demand and channel-inventory indices (like JODI for oil).
why: Double-ordering and hoarding amplify a ~10-15% supply gap into a 4x price spike; transparency deflates phantom demand and lets fabs plan capacity; attacks effective supply.

title: One copy of each AI model per rack via content-addressed pooling
idea: Po: there is only one copy of every model. Inference hosts serving the same open-weight model map its weights read-only from a content-addressed (hash per 2 MB page) CXL memory pool shared across tenants and GPUs, instead of each VM loading its own copy into host DRAM.
why: Popular models are replicated dozens of times per rack in host memory; dedup frees ~30-60% of host DRAM on inference fleets; attacks usable capacity per installed bit.

title: Convert idle NAND fabs into stacked DRAM-class memory lines
idea: Po: the NAND fab is a DRAM fab. NAND lines already build 200+-layer stacks with zero EUV using high-aspect-ratio etch, staircase contacts and ALD; a stacked-tier DRAM-class cell (horizontal capacitor tiers sharing a vertical bitline) is designed to reuse >80% of that tool set, so NAND overcapacity is converted rather than new fabs built.
why: Conversion costs a fraction of a $15B greenfield and takes ~1-2 years; tier count, not lithography, buys density; attacks capital intensity and EUV dependence.

title: Capacity cascade moving legacy DRAM to depreciated DUV fabs
idea: Po: the oldest fab cures the newest shortage. Auto, industrial and set-top demand for DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 is contractually migrated to fully depreciated 25-38 nm ArF fabs (including revived shuttered lines) under swap agreements: the advanced-node maker gets the freed wafer starts, the old-fab operator gets long-term qualified volume.
why: Legacy grades still occupy a meaningful share of advanced wafers; freeing them for DDR5/HBM adds capacity with no new EUV tools, and depreciated fabs sell bits near cash cost; attacks capital intensity.

title: Gridded one-direction layouts for every DRAM layer
idea: Po: the chip only has straight lines. Array and periphery are redesigned so every critical layer is unidirectional lines on a fixed pitch made by self-aligned quadruple patterning, with shapes defined only by DUV cut masks; a gridded 1D periphery cell library replaces 2D shapes.
why: 1D patterns print reliably at ~18-20 nm half pitch with ArF immersion, recovering most of EUV's density; mask count rises modestly while ~$150-380M per avoided EUV scanner is saved; attacks capital and single-supplier risk.

title: Nanoimprint stamps for DRAM array layers, DUV for periphery
idea: Po: masks are rubber stamps. The highly periodic array layers (active, buried wordline, bitline, storage-node contact) are patterned by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from e-beam-written master templates, while irregular periphery stays on ArF immersion with mix-and-match alignment.
why: Imprint tools cost a fraction of EUV and use ~10x less power; array redundancy absorbs NIL's isolated defects; attacks capital intensity and energy.

title: Block copolymer self-assembly prints hexagonal capacitor arrays
idea: Po: chips are grown, not made. A cylinder-forming high-chi block copolymer self-assembles into a hexagonal lattice matching the DRAM capacitor honeycomb; a coarse ArF guide pattern at 3x pitch registers it (density multiplication), and the cylinders become the hard mask for storage-node holes.
why: Defines the densest DRAM layer without EUV or quadruple patterning, saving ~3-4 litho/etch passes; attacks litho capital.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina pores as capacitor hole templates
idea: Po: aluminum drills the holes. A deposited aluminum film is two-step anodized so self-ordering yields hexagonal nanopores at 40-60 nm pitch with aspect ratios over 100:1; pore registry is seeded by a DUV-patterned pre-texture, and the alumina template is lined TiN/high-k/TiN to form storage capacitors.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (needs AR ~115) while removing EUV and the hardest high-aspect-ratio etch, using room-temperature electrochemistry; attacks capital and density.

title: Maskless laser interference lithography for periodic array gratings
idea: Po: light writes its own grating. A compact 193 nm (or 213 nm solid-state) multi-beam immersion interference exposure prints line/space and hex-dot gratings across the wafer with no mask and no projection lens; a cheap KrF/i-line step trims gratings into arrays and patterns periphery.
why: Interference tools are mostly lasers and prisms (~1/20 the cost of a scanner) yet reach the 30-40 nm pitches arrays need; attacks capital intensity and single-supplier risk.

title: Multi-beam e-beam direct write for cut and contact layers
idea: Po: a million pens instead of one camera. Mask-writer-class multi-beam e-beam columns (~250k beamlets) write only the sparse cut and contact layers directly on wafers while dense lines come from spacer patterning; no masks are needed, so micro-fabs and fast design spins become economical.
why: Cut/contact layers are the ones that otherwise force EUV; writing them maskless avoids EUV and multi-million-dollar mask sets, with throughput suited to ~5-10k wafers/month micro-fabs; attacks capital and U.S. micro-fab viability.

title: Regional patterning hub serving several small DRAM fabs
idea: Po: the scanner is a public library. One shared facility runs the ArF immersion critical-layer exposures for 3-5 nearby small fabs; wafers travel in sealed N2 FOUPs on a scheduled shuttle, and each satellite fab owns only cheaper deposition, etch, CMP and KrF tools.
why: Litho is the costliest tool class; pooling raises scanner utilization from ~60% to ~90% and makes 5k-wafer-per-month micro-fabs viable; attacks capital intensity.

title: Tool bank of displaced immersion scanners leased to new entrants
idea: Po: the scanner nobody wants is the treasure. A fund buys ArF immersion scanners and multi-patterning track/etch sets displaced as logic fabs migrate to EUV, refurbishes them to spec, and leases them to new DRAM entrants with guaranteed service contracts.
why: Used immersion tools cost a fraction of new and skip allocation queues, turning a 2-3-year tool lead time into months; attacks capital and time.

title: Pay-per-wafer-pass equipment leasing from toolmakers
idea: Po: the toolmaker owns the fab. DUV scanner, etch and deposition OEMs keep ownership of their tools inside the DRAM fab and bill per wafer pass with uptime guarantees; the operator carries only building, people and materials.
why: Moves depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) off the entrant's balance sheet and ties OEM revenue to yield and uptime; cuts the entry ticket for a 20k-wafer fab by billions; attacks capital intensity.

title: Turnkey EUV-free DRAM fab franchise
idea: Po: a fab is a burger franchise. A franchisor packages a frozen EUV-free DRAM process (DUV plus self-aligned patterning), tool list, recipes, yield-learning database, training academy and a qualification brand; regional franchisees (states, sovereign funds, consortia) build identical fabs and pay royalties per wafer.
why: Copy-exactly replication shrinks yield ramp from years to months and lets capacity grow in parallel without EUV allocation; attacks capital, time and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Array wafer plus foundry periphery wafer joined by hybrid bonding
idea: Po: one chip is two chips from two countries. A DUV-only DRAM fab makes array-only wafers, while a U.S. 28/22 nm logic foundry makes the periphery wafer; the two are wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonded so the ~49% periphery sits under the array.
why: Uses idle mature logic capacity, shrinks DRAM die area up to ~40%, and lets the array fab skip high-performance transistor steps; attacks periphery overhead, capital and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Sequential layer-transfer tiers re-patterned with the same DUV masks
idea: Po: the wafer grows a new wafer every week. After a DRAM array tier is finished, a thin single-crystal Si sheet is transferred on top by ion-cut at <400 C and the same DUV mask set builds the next tier with laser-annealed low-temperature transistors; four tiers quadruple bits per area with no pitch shrink.
why: Density by tier count rather than lithography, reusing one mask set; attacks EUV dependence and cost per bit if per-tier yield exceeds ~95%.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM slabs from mature DUV nodes
idea: Po: the wafer is the chip. A 25 nm-class DUV DRAM wafer is never diced: on-wafer redundancy, a wafer-level routing mesh and a bonded controller tile expose the whole wafer (~0.5 TB) as one memory slab for rack-level CXL pools, with bad mats mapped out at test.
why: Skips dicing, packaging and module assembly (~15-25% of cost) and lets older DUV fabs supply capacity-tier memory; attacks capital and cost per bit.

title: Two-bit-per-cell DRAM using relaxed-pitch fat capacitors
idea: Po: bigger cells hold more bits. With EUV forbidden, cells stay at ~20 nm-class pitch but capacitors grow to ~15-20 fF; that charge budget supports four-level storage read by a two-step sense amplifier against a reference ladder, giving 2 bits per cell.
why: Doubling bits per cell offsets the ~1.5-2x area penalty of skipping EUV; attacks density and cost per bit with no new litho, but sense margin and refresh risk are high.

title: Vertical-channel 4F2 cells at relaxed DUV pitch
idea: Po: density comes from area, not pitch. A vertical-channel transistor with buried bitline and surrounding-gate wordline gives a 4F2 cell; at F=18 nm (reachable by SAQP on ArF immersion) the cell is 1,296 nm2, equal to a 6F2 cell at ~14.7 nm, a node that otherwise needs EUV.
why: Matches next-node density using DUV only; attacks litho capital and EUV dependence.

title: Area-selective deposition replaces landing-pad and contact lithography
idea: Po: the material patterns only where it wants. Self-assembled monolayer inhibitors block growth on dielectric so ALD metal nucleates only on exposed silicon/TiN, forming self-aligned landing pads and contacts that previously needed a critical litho layer; a selective etch-back removes stray nuclei.
why: Removes 2-3 critical patterning steps and their overlay errors without EUV; attacks litho capital and cycle time.

title: DNA-brick templates position contact holes at 15 nm pitch
idea: Po: DNA draws the circuit. DNA-brick crystals self-assemble onto DUV-defined binding sites carrying metal-oxide precursors, which are converted into a hard mask for contact or capacitor holes at ~15 nm pitch; the DNA is burned off before high-temperature steps.
why: Benchtop self-assembly gives sub-EUV feature placement; attacks capital intensity, though placement error and contamination are speculative.

title: DRAM-only 450 mm fab reviving immersion 450 prototypes
idea: Po: the wafer is twice as big. The 450 mm transition stalled partly because EUV never had a 450 mm version; a DUV-only DRAM fab revives the 450 mm immersion scanner and process-tool prototypes from the G450C era and runs DRAM wafers with 2.25x the area per wafer pass.
why: Past estimates promised ~20-30% lower cost per die at 450 mm; DRAM's single-product volume justifies a dedicated tool set; attacks cost per bit and capital per bit.

title: Revive deep-trench eDRAM as standalone memory chiplets
idea: Po: the logic foundry already makes DRAM. Deep-trench capacitor eDRAM, proven on 32-14 nm SOI logic lines without EUV, is turned into standalone 4-8 Gb capacity chiplets with simplified periphery, built on existing U.S. logic lines and sold via CXL or UCIe.
why: Taps idle mature U.S. logic capacity for DRAM-class memory; ~10+ fF trench caps extend retention; attacks U.S. manufacturability and supplier diversity at some density penalty.

title: Advance market commitment for EUV-free domestic DRAM
idea: Po: the government buys DRAM that does not exist yet. Like vaccine advance market commitments, the U.S. guarantees to buy a set volume (e.g., 1 EB/year for federal and defense fleets) at a fixed price from any domestic producer whose process uses no EUV, paying only on delivery of qualified parts.
why: Removes demand risk for new entrants and hedges the single EUV supplier, paying only for results; attacks capital risk and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Slow capacity-tier DRAM with mega-mats to shrink periphery
idea: Po: memory is cheaper because it is slower. Since cells cannot shrink without EUV, periphery shrinks instead: a capacity-tier DRAM uses 2-4x longer bitlines and wordlines per mat, larger pages and fewer sense amplifiers, accepting ~2x tRCD for 150-250 ns CXL-attached memory, with fat DUV capacitors keeping Cs/Cbl workable.
why: Cuts periphery from ~49% to ~25-30% of die, raising bits per wafer ~30-40%; attacks density and cost per bit.
